metadata.title: Factor Graphs and the Sum-Product Algorithm
metadata.authors: F. R. Kschischang, B. J. Frey, H.-A. Loeliger
metadata.venue: IEEE Transactions on Information Theory, Vol. 47, No. 2
metadata.source_note: Extracted from PDF→text fallback; .tex source not available. Math fidelity reduced — inline mathematical symbols, subscripts, and equation right-hand sides were largely stripped or garbled by the PDF extractor. Statements give natural-language paraphrases with best-effort LaTeX where the symbols are recoverable from context.

nodes.name: Marginal function (summary)
nodes.statement: Given $f(x_1,\dots,x_n)$, the marginal function $g_i(x_i)$ is the sum of $f$ over all variables except $x_i$. The paper introduces the “not-sum” / “summary” notation that lists the variables NOT summed over.
nodes.statement_clean: The i-th marginal of f is obtained by summing out every variable except x_i; the paper writes this as a 'summary for x_i'.

nodes.name: Factor graph
nodes.statement: A factor graph is a bipartite graph representing the factorization $f(x_1,\dots,x_n)=\prod_{j\in J} f_j(X_j)$, with one variable node per $x_i$, one factor node per $f_j$, and an edge between variable $x_i$ and factor $f_j$ iff $x_i\in X_j$.
nodes.statement_clean: A bipartite graph whose two node classes are variables and local factors, with edges encoding 'is an argument of'.

nodes.name: Expression tree
nodes.statement: An ordered rooted tree whose internal vertices are arithmetic operators and whose leaves are variables, constants, or (in the paper's extension) local functions; it represents an arithmetic expression.

nodes.name: Iverson's convention / characteristic function
nodes.statement: For a predicate $P$, $[P]$ is the indicator equal to $1$ if $P$ is true and $0$ otherwise. For a behavior $B\subseteq \mathcal{S}$, the characteristic function $\chi_B(s) = [s\in B]$.
nodes.statement_clean: Indicator of a predicate or membership; equals 1 when true, 0 otherwise.

nodes.name: Behavior / behavioral model
nodes.statement: A behavior $B$ in configuration space $\mathcal{S}=A_1\times\cdots\times A_n$ is any subset of $\mathcal{S}$; its elements are the valid configurations. A block code of length $n$ over alphabet $A$ is a behavior in $A^n$.

nodes.name: Tanner graph
nodes.statement: Factor graph of the characteristic function of a linear code defined by a parity-check matrix $H$: variable nodes correspond to columns of $H$, factor (check) nodes to rows of $H$, with an edge wherever $H_{ij}\neq 0$.

nodes.name: Wiberg-type graph (hidden / state variables)
nodes.statement: A factor graph that augments the visible variables with hidden (auxiliary, latent, state) variables; a graph for behavior $\widetilde B$ also represents the visible behavior $B$ obtained by projecting onto the visible variables.

nodes.name: Trellis (for a block code)
nodes.statement: An edge-labeled directed graph with distinguished root and goal vertices such that the codewords of $C$ are exactly the sequences of edge labels along directed root–goal paths, with all root-to-vertex paths of equal length (the depth).

nodes.name: APP distribution (a posteriori probability)
nodes.statement: For a codeword $X$ transmitted over a memoryless channel with output $Y=y$ fixed, the joint APP distribution of the codeword symbols is proportional to $p(X)\,p(y\mid X) \propto \chi_C(X)\prod_i p(y_i\mid x_i)$.

nodes.name: Semiring (for the sum-product algorithm)
nodes.statement: An algebraic structure with two operations “$+$” and “$\cdot$” satisfying the distributive law $a\cdot(b+c)=a\cdot b+a\cdot c$. The codomain of the global function may be any such semiring.

nodes.name: Min-sum and max-product semirings
nodes.statement: The max-product semiring replaces real summation by $\max$; the min-sum semiring (in the negative log-likelihood domain) replaces product by sum and $\max$ by $\min$. Both satisfy the distributive law required by the sum-product algorithm.

nodes.name: Message-passing schedule
nodes.statement: Specification of which messages are passed during each clock tick. Examples: flooding schedule (every direction of every edge each tick); serial schedule (at most one message per tick). A message is “pending” at edge $e$ when new messages have arrived since the last transmission on $e$.

nodes.name: LDPC code
nodes.statement: A code defined by a regular bipartite graph in which left (variable) nodes have degree $j$ and right (check) nodes have degree $k$; checks enforce even parity over their adjacent symbols.

nodes.name: Repeat–accumulate (RA) code
nodes.statement: A low-complexity turbo-like code whose encoder repeats each input bit $q$ times, permutes the result, and feeds the permuted stream into an accumulator $x_i = x_{i-1}\oplus z_i$.

nodes.name: Probability parametrizations for binary variables (LR, LLR, LD, SLLD)
nodes.statement: Four parametrizations of a Bernoulli distribution: likelihood ratio $LR=p_0/p_1$, log-likelihood ratio $LLR=\log(p_0/p_1)$, likelihood difference $LD=p_0-p_1$, and signed log-likelihood difference $SLLD$ (sign and log-magnitude of the difference).

nodes.name: Spanning tree of a connected graph
nodes.statement: A connected, cycle-free subgraph of $G$ having the same vertex set as $G$.

nodes.name: Markov random field (MRF)
nodes.statement: A graphical model on an undirected graph $G=(V,E)$ in which each vertex carries a random variable and the joint distribution satisfies the local Markov property: every variable is independent of nonneighbors given its neighbors.

nodes.name: Bayesian network
nodes.statement: A graphical model on a directed acyclic graph in which the joint distribution factors as $p(x_1,\dots,x_n) = \prod_i p(x_i\mid x_{a(i)})$, where $a(i)$ is the parent set of vertex $i$.

nodes.name: DFT kernel
nodes.statement: For a complex-valued $N$-tuple $f$, the discrete Fourier transform is $F_k=\sum_n f_n\,W^{nk}$ where $W=e^{-2\pi i/N}$ is a primitive $N$-th root of unity.

nodes.name: MPF (marginalize product-of-functions) problem
nodes.statement: Given a function $f(x_1,\dots,x_n)$ that factors as $\prod_{j} f_j(X_j)$, efficiently compute one or all of the marginal functions $g_i(x_i)$.
nodes.statement_clean: Compute marginals of a globally complicated function that factors into local pieces.

nodes.name: Maximum-likelihood sequence detection (MLSD)
nodes.statement: Find the codeword (or hidden-variable configuration) that maximizes the a posteriori probability, equivalently $\arg\max_x f(x)$ where $f$ factors over a trellis or factor graph.

nodes.name: Iterative decoding of turbo / LDPC codes
nodes.statement: Approximate symbol-wise APP decoding of long codes (turbo, LDPC, RA) whose factor graphs contain cycles, performed by running the sum-product algorithm despite the cycles.

nodes.name: Computing the discrete Fourier transform
nodes.statement: Given $f\in\mathbb{C}^N$, compute the DFT vector $F$ defined by $F_k=\sum_n f_n W^{nk}$, $W=e^{-2\pi i/N}$.

nodes.name: Single-i sum-product algorithm
nodes.statement: On a rooted cycle-free factor graph (root variable $x_i$), bottom-up message passing that computes the single marginal $g_i(x_i)$ as the product of all messages arriving at the root.
input: A cycle-free factor graph for $f$
A distinguished variable node $x_i$ to serve as root
output: The marginal function $g_i(x_i)$ as the product of all messages received at the root

nodes.name: Sum-product algorithm
nodes.statement: Generic message-passing algorithm: each node sends, on edge $e$, the product of its local function (or unit, if a variable node) with the most recent messages received on every other incident edge, summarized for the variable of $e$.
input: A factor graph for $f(x_1,\dots,x_n)=\prod_j f_j(X_j)$
A message-passing schedule (cycle-free graphs admit a finite leaves-to-root-to-leaves schedule)
output: All marginal functions $g_i(x_i)$ as products of incoming messages at variable node $x_i$ (exact when the factor graph is cycle-free)

nodes.name: Forward/backward (BCJR / APP / MAP) algorithm
nodes.statement: Sum-product algorithm specialized to the cycle-free factor graph of a hidden Markov model / trellis: a forward recursion computes $\alpha$-messages, a backward recursion computes $\beta$-messages, and per-section APPs are products of $\alpha,\beta$ and the channel likelihood.
input: Trellis / hidden Markov factor graph
Channel observations $y$ (regarded as parameters)
output: Per-section a posteriori probabilities for state and symbol variables

nodes.name: Viterbi algorithm
nodes.statement: Sum-product algorithm in the min-sum semiring on a trellis factor graph: a forward (and optionally backward) recursion of “minimum of sums” computes the maximum-likelihood codeword.
input: Trellis factor graph with branch metrics (e.g. squared Euclidean or Hamming distance)
Channel observations
nodes.origin_citation: Viterbi (cf. paper's discussion of min-sum semiring)

nodes.name: Kalman filter
nodes.statement: Sum-product algorithm on the cycle-free factor graph of a discrete-time linear Gaussian state-space model, using integration as the summary operator; messages are Gaussian and parametrized by mean and variance, yielding the standard Kalman prediction and update equations.
input: Linear Gaussian state-space model (state, input, output, noise scalars or vectors)
Sequence of observations $y_1,y_2,\dots$
output: MMSE state estimates $\hat x_k$ and prediction/update mean–variance pairs

nodes.name: Iterative turbo decoder as sum-product
nodes.statement: Iterative decoding of a parallel concatenated convolutional (turbo) code via a flooding-style schedule that alternates forward/backward passes over each constituent code's trellis with extrinsic-message exchanges through the interleaver.
input: Turbo-code factor graph (two trellises linked by an interleaver permutation $\pi$)
Channel observations of systematic and parity sequences
output: Approximate symbol APPs for the information bits (after a finite number of iterations)

nodes.name: Sum-product / belief-propagation decoding of LDPC codes
nodes.statement: Run the sum-product algorithm on the (Tanner) factor graph of an LDPC code under a flooding schedule; at variable nodes, multiply incoming messages, at parity-check nodes apply (21).
input: LDPC parity-check matrix / Tanner graph
Channel log-likelihoods for each codeword bit
output: Approximate per-bit APPs and a decoded codeword

nodes.name: FFT as sum-product on a transformed factor graph
nodes.statement: Express variables of the DFT in binary, draw the factor graph of the DFT kernel, choose a spanning tree, then apply the clustering and stretching transformations of Section VI; running the sum-product algorithm on the resulting cycle-free graph computes the DFT in $O(N\log N)$ multiply-and-accumulate operations.
input: Length-$N=2^n$ complex sequence $f$
Spanning tree of the DFT factor graph and the corresponding clustering/stretching choices
output: DFT vector $F$ obtained as marginals on the cycle-free transformed factor graph (an FFT)

nodes.name: Pearl's belief propagation (in a Bayesian network)
nodes.statement: Variable-to-variable message passing in a Bayesian network using $\pi$-messages (downward, from parents) and $\lambda$-messages (upward, from children); the belief at each node is the product of all $\pi$ and $\lambda$ messages it receives.
input: Bayesian network with conditional probability tables $p(x_i\mid x_{a(i)})$
Observed evidence on a subset of variables
output: Belief BEL$(x)$ – posterior marginal of each variable given the evidence

nodes.name: Clustering transformation
nodes.statement: Merge two like-typed nodes (two variables, or two function nodes) of a factor graph into a single node representing the pair; preserves the global function and may eliminate cycles, at the cost of larger alphabets / heavier local functions.
input: Factor graph and a pair of nodes $(u,v)$ of the same type to cluster
output: Equivalent factor graph in which $u,v$ are replaced by a single node $(u,v)$

nodes.name: Stretching transformation
nodes.statement: Pair a variable $x$ with a neighbouring variable $z$ at distance two (and modify intervening function nodes), “stretching” $x$ along a path; iteratively stretching $x$ around a cycle and deleting the resulting redundant edge breaks the cycle.
input: Factor graph and a variable $x$ to stretch along a chosen path / cycle
output: Equivalent factor graph in which $x$ is represented at multiple paired nodes; combined with edge-deletion, can convert the graph to cycle-free form

nodes.name: Cycle-free factor graphs encode marginal expressions
nodes.statement: When a factor graph for $f(x_1,\dots,x_n)=\prod_j f_j(X_j)$ is cycle-free (a factor tree), the graph itself encodes an arithmetic expression for each marginal $g_i(x_i)$: rooting the tree at $x_i$, replacing variable nodes by products and factor nodes by “multiply by $f_j$ then summarize” operators yields an expression tree for $g_i$.
conclusions: The factor graph admits a rooted-tree transformation into an expression tree computing $g_i(x_i)$
Hence the sum-product algorithm computes $g_i$ exactly on cycle-free factor graphs

nodes.name: Distributive law over a semiring extends sum-product
nodes.statement: If the codomain of $f$ is a (commutative) semiring with operations satisfying $a\cdot(b+c)=a\cdot b+a\cdot c$, then the sum-product algorithm and the cycle-free correctness result of TP378.1 carry over verbatim to that semiring (e.g. max-product, min-sum).
assumptions: Codomain is a semiring with distributive law $a\cdot(b+c)=a\cdot b+a\cdot c$
conclusions: Cycle-free sum-product on this semiring computes the corresponding semiring marginals exactly

nodes.name: Every code admits a cycle-free factor graph (via trellises)
nodes.statement: Since every block code has a trellis representation, and a factor graph corresponding to a trellis is cycle-free, every code admits a cycle-free factor graph representation – although the state-space sizes can be impractically large (motivating graphs with cycles).
conclusions: $C$ has a cycle-free factor graph representation
State alphabets of this representation may be prohibitively large in practice

nodes.name: Iverson factorization for conjunctions
nodes.statement: If $P=P_1\wedge P_2\wedge\cdots\wedge P_k$, then $[P]=\prod_i [P_i]$ (in $\{0,1\}$). Hence a behavior defined by a conjunction of local checks factorizes, and is naturally represented by a factor graph.
assumptions: Predicate $P$ is a logical conjunction of predicates $P_1,\dots,P_k$
conclusions: The corresponding behavior decomposes as a product of local characteristic functions

nodes.name: Variable nodes of degree two perform no computation
nodes.statement: In the sum-product algorithm, a variable node of degree two simply passes the message arriving on one edge through to the other edge unchanged.
assumptions: Variable node $x$ has exactly two incident edges in the factor graph
conclusions: The outgoing message on either edge equals the incoming message on the opposite edge

nodes.name: Spanning-tree marginalization with stretching
nodes.statement: Let $T$ be a spanning tree of a connected factor graph $G$. If every variable $x$ is stretched along all paths in $T$ from $x$ to every function node having $x$ as an argument, then every edge of $G$ not in $T$ is redundant and may be deleted, yielding a cycle-free factor graph on which sum-product computes exact marginals.
assumptions: Each variable $x$ has been stretched along all relevant paths in $T$
conclusions: All edges of $G$ outside $T$ are redundant and can be deleted
Sum-product on the resulting cycle-free graph yields exact marginals (this matches the junction-tree condition)

nodes.name: Equivalence of MRF / Bayesian network factorizations with factor graphs
nodes.statement: Both Markov random fields (Gibbs / clique factorization, $p(x)=\prod_{c}\psi_c(x_c)/Z$) and Bayesian networks (parent-conditional factorization, $p(x)=\prod_i p(x_i\mid x_{a(i)})$) yield distributions whose factorization can be represented by a factor graph; consequently Pearl's belief propagation is an instance of the sum-product algorithm.
assumptions: Distribution $p$ is given by an MRF Gibbs factorization or a Bayesian-network parent factorization
conclusions: Pearl's belief-propagation rules can be derived from the sum-product update equations

nodes.name: Sum-product update at a variable node
nodes.statement: $\mu_{x\to f}(x) = \prod_{h\in n(x)\setminus\{f\}} \mu_{h\to x}(x)$ – message from variable $x$ to neighbouring factor $f$ is the product of incoming messages from all other neighbours of $x$.

nodes.name: Sum-product update at a factor node
nodes.statement: $\mu_{f\to x}(x) = \sum_{\sim\{x\}}\Big( f(X_f)\prod_{y\in n(f)\setminus\{x\}}\mu_{y\to f}(y)\Big)$ – multiply $f$ by incoming messages from other variable neighbours, then summarize for $x$.

nodes.name: Forward/backward recursion in trellis sum-product
nodes.statement: $\alpha_k(s_k) = \sum_{e:\,s_k(e)=s_k} \alpha_{k-1}(s_{k-1}(e))\,\gamma_k(e)$ and a symmetric backward recursion for $\beta$, summed over edges $e$ in trellis section $k$ with branch metric $\gamma_k$.

nodes.name: Min-sum (Viterbi) update
nodes.statement: $\widetilde\alpha_k(s_k) = \min_{e:\,s_k(e)=s_k}\big(\widetilde\alpha_{k-1}(s_{k-1}(e)) + \widetilde\gamma_k(e)\big)$ – “minimum of sums” replacing the “sum of products”.

nodes.name: Binary variable-node sum-product update
nodes.statement: For two incoming binary messages $(p^a_0,p^a_1),(p^b_0,p^b_1)$ at a variable node of degree three, the outgoing message is $(p^a_0 p^b_0,\,p^a_1 p^b_1)/Z$.

nodes.name: Binary parity-check sum-product update
nodes.statement: At a check node enforcing $x_1\oplus x_2\oplus x_3=0$ with two incoming messages, the outgoing message has $p_0 = p^a_0 p^b_0 + p^a_1 p^b_1$ and $p_1 = p^a_0 p^b_1 + p^a_1 p^b_0$.

nodes.name: Belief-propagation belief update
nodes.statement: $\mathrm{BEL}(x) \propto \lambda(x)\,\pi(x)$, the product of all $\lambda$- and $\pi$-messages received at variable $x$ in Pearl's belief propagation; this equals the product of incoming messages at $x$ in the corresponding factor graph.

nodes.name: DFT formula
nodes.statement: $F_k = \sum_{n=0}^{N-1} f_n\,W^{nk}$ with $W = e^{-2\pi i /N}$.

nodes.name: Simple factor graph (Example 1)
nodes.statement: Function $f(x_1,\dots,x_5) = f_A(x_1)\,f_B(x_2)\,f_C(x_1,x_2,x_3)\,f_D(x_3,x_4)\,f_E(x_3,x_5)$ and its factor graph (Fig. 1), used as a running example for the sum-product computation of marginals.

nodes.name: Tanner graph for a binary linear code (Example 2)
nodes.statement: A binary $(n=6,k=3)$ linear code defined by an explicit $3\times 6$ parity-check matrix $H$; the characteristic function factors as a product of three parity checks, giving a Tanner graph (Fig. 8).

nodes.name: Trellis description (Example 3)
nodes.statement: Trellis representation of the code of Example 2 and the corresponding Wiberg-type factor graph with hidden state variables; each trellis section contributes one local check.

nodes.name: Linear time-invariant state-space model (Example 4)
nodes.statement: Classical LTI state-space equations $s_{k+1} = A s_k + B u_k$, $y_k = C s_k + D u_k$ recast as a factor graph (Fig. 10) with one trellis section per time step.

nodes.name: APP distributions for a memoryless channel (Example 5)
nodes.statement: For a codeword $X\in C$ transmitted over a memoryless channel with output $y$, the APP distribution factors as $\chi_C(X)\prod_i p(y_i\mid x_i)$, illustrated for the code of Example 2 (Fig. 11).

nodes.name: Markov chain and hidden Markov model (Example 6)
nodes.statement: Joint distribution of $x_1,\dots,x_n$ that forms a Markov chain factors as $p(x_1)\prod_{k\ge 2} p(x_k\mid x_{k-1})$; observing $x_k$ through a memoryless channel adds emission factors $p(y_k\mid x_k)$, giving the hidden Markov model factor graph (Fig. 12).

nodes.name: Turbo code factor graph (Section V-B)
nodes.statement: Factor graph of a (short) parallel concatenated convolutional code, with two constituent encoder trellises linked by an interleaver permutation $\pi$ (Fig. 16); the graph contains a cycle through the interleaver.

nodes.name: LDPC code factor graph (Section V-C)
nodes.statement: Tanner-style factor graph of a small $(j,k)$-regular LDPC code (Fig. 17), illustrating left/right degree regularity.

nodes.name: Repeat–accumulate code factor graph (Section V-D)
nodes.statement: Two equivalent factor graphs for an RA encoder (Fig. 18): the direct graph using $\bmod\,2$ check nodes, and the variant using equality constraints to express the same code more compactly.

nodes.name: DFT / FFT factor graph (Section VI-D)
nodes.statement: Factor graph of the $N=8$ DFT kernel (Fig. 22a), one of its spanning trees (Fig. 22b), and the cycle-free factor graph after clustering and stretching (Fig. 22c) on which the sum-product algorithm computes the FFT.

nodes.name: MRF / Bayesian network / factor graph comparison
nodes.statement: A common probability distribution displayed as (a) a Markov random field, (b) a Bayesian network, and (c) a factor graph (Fig. 24), illustrating how the same factorization is captured in each formalism.

nodes.name: Sum-product on cyclic graphs is approximate
nodes.statement: On factor graphs with cycles the sum-product algorithm has no natural termination, messages traverse each edge repeatedly, and the resulting outputs cannot in general be interpreted as exact function summaries; nevertheless turbo / LDPC results show striking empirical accuracy.

nodes.name: Stretching can break all cycles
nodes.statement: By systematically stretching variables around cycles and deleting resulting redundant edges, an arbitrary factor graph can be converted into an equivalent cycle-free factor graph (matching the junction-tree property), at the cost of larger variable alphabets.

nodes.name: Pedagogical advantage of factor graphs over BP
nodes.statement: Pearl's $\pi/\lambda$ belief-update rules become noticeably more elaborate than the single sum-product update rule – a pedagogical motivation for working with factor graphs rather than directly with Bayesian networks.

nodes.name: Proof of TP378.1 (factor tree to expression tree)
nodes.statement: By recursive application of the distributive law on the rooted factor tree: each subtree's contribution to the marginal $g_i$ is the summary for $x_i$ of the product of its local functions, computed independently and combined at the root.

nodes.name: Decompose $f$ at the root
nodes.statement: Root the factor tree at $x_i$; write $f = \prod_{h\in n(x_i)} F_h$, where $F_h$ is the product of all local functions in the subtree rooted at the $h$-th neighbour of $x_i$ and the subtrees have pairwise-disjoint variable sets.

nodes.name: Apply the distributive law to factor the summary
nodes.statement: By the distributive law, the summary for $x_i$ of a product over disjoint variable sets equals the product of the summaries: $\sum_{\sim\{x_i\}} f \;=\; \prod_{h} \sum_{\sim\{x_i\}} F_h$.

nodes.name: Recurse into each subtree
nodes.statement: Each summary $\sum_{\sim\{x_i\}} F_h$ is a problem of the same form on the smaller subtree rooted at $h$, so the same decomposition recursively applies until leaves are reached.

nodes.name: Identify recursion with the expression tree
nodes.statement: The recursion's structure matches the local substitutions of Fig. 5 (variable node → product, factor node → multiply by $f$ then summarize), which is precisely the rooted-tree-to-expression-tree transformation; hence sum-product computes $g_i$ exactly.

nodes.name: Sketch: spanning-tree edges outside $T$ are redundant
nodes.statement: For any edge $e=(x',f)\notin T$, every variable in $X_f\setminus\{x'\}$ has been stretched along its $T$-path to a neighbour of $f$, so $X_f$ is fully covered by the variable sets on the remaining edges of $f$ – hence $e$ is redundant and can be deleted.
